what: Lear makes car seats and electrical systems. Its seating business supplies complete seats to carmakers, and its electrical business makes the wiring harnesses, connectors and electronics that distribute power and data around a vehicle. Both are designed into specific vehicle platforms.
customers: Carmakers worldwide, who specify Lear components during vehicle development and buy them for the model’s entire production run.
money: Complete seat systems, seat structures and components.
Wiring harnesses, connection systems and electronic control modules.
moat: A seat or wiring harness is engineered specifically for one vehicle platform and qualified for it, so once a programme is won the revenue is secured for the model’s production life — typically five to seven years. Seats are also bulky and expensive to ship, so suppliers build plants next to the carmaker’s assembly line, which creates physical as well as commercial lock-in.
risks: Last year’s net margin was 1.9%, which is the structural reality of being a large automotive supplier: powerful customers negotiate the margin away.
Revenue has been flat at about $23.3B for three years, and depends entirely on carmakers’ production volumes.
Debt of $3.5B against $1.0B of cash is meaningful for a business with margins this thin.
Carmakers routinely demand annual price reductions from suppliers, which is a permanent headwind.
Fourteen analysts average a $145.93 target against a $106.16 price, a 38% gap.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 9.3 times earnings, 4.8 times EV/EBITDA, 0.22 times sales and 7.3 times free cash flow.
Free cash flow of $700.8M against a $5.1B market value is a 13.7% yield.
Electric vehicles need more wiring and power electronics content, not less, which favours the E-Systems business.
Programme wins secure revenue for a vehicle’s entire production life, which makes future revenue visible.
Trailing net income of $584.4M is a substantial improvement on the low-margin year.
watch: Content per vehicle and the backlog of new programme awards. Production volumes are outside Lear’s control; content and new wins are what management affects.
view: Being a large automotive supplier is one of the harder commercial positions in manufacturing, and Lear’s 1.9% net margin last year shows why. The customers are a handful of enormous carmakers who know exactly what a seat costs to make, who demand annual price reductions as a condition of the contract, and who can move a programme to a competitor at the next model cycle. Scale does not fix this; it is the structure of the relationship.

What Lear does have is visibility and physical entrenchment. A seat system is engineered for one specific vehicle platform, qualified for it, and then built in a plant located next to the carmaker’s assembly line — because seats are too bulky to ship far. That means once a programme is won, the revenue is secured for the model’s production life, and the supplier relationship has a physical dimension that is genuinely hard to unwind mid-cycle.

The electrification question runs in Lear’s favour, which is worth stating because the instinct is the opposite. An electric vehicle needs more wiring, more power distribution and more electronic control than a combustion one, so the E-Systems business grows in content per vehicle as the fleet changes. Seating is broadly neutral. Lear is not one of the suppliers whose product disappears with the engine.

At 9.3 times earnings, 4.8 times EV/EBITDA, 0.22 times sales and a 13.7% free cash flow yield, the market is pricing this as a structurally challenged business in a weak production environment. The first part is fair and permanent; the second is cyclical. With $3.5 billion of debt against a 2% margin there is not much room for error, so this is a cheap cyclical rather than a compounder. Content per vehicle and new programme awards are the two numbers management actually controls.
bull: Rising electrical content per vehicle meets a production recovery, and a 13.7% free cash flow yield on 0.22 times sales rerates substantially.
bear: Carmakers keep extracting annual price reductions from a 2% margin business, production stays weak, and $3.5 billion of debt leaves no cushion.
